lines.text: Some of the world's first farmers, hundreds of peoples and languages, colonial rule and a hard-fought war. This is the story of Papua New Guinea.
About nine thousand years ago, people in the highland swamps at Kuk were already tending gardens, among the first farmers anywhere on Earth.
In 1873 the explorer John Moresby named a harbour on the south coast after his father. Port Moresby is now the capital.
In 1884 Germany claimed the north of the eastern half of the island, and German New Guinea lasted until after the First World War.
Britain took the south, and from 1906 Australia ran it as the Territory of Papua, and later took over the German north as well.
Michael Somare, born in 1936, would lead the push for self-rule and become the first prime minister, the father of the nation.
In 1942, along the Kokoda Track over the mountains, Australian soldiers stopped the Japanese advance on Port Moresby.
James Marape, born in 1971 in the highlands, would become prime minister in 2019.
In 1975 Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia, a nation of hundreds of languages on the eastern half of the island and its islands.
In 1988 a quarrel over a copper mine on Bougainville turned into a war that lasted a decade.
In 2019, under the peace that ended it, the people of Bougainville voted, and they chose independence.
And in May 2024, in the highlands of Enga, a landslide buried a village under rock and earth.
From the gardens of Kuk to a young nation of many peoples, Papua New Guinea's story goes on.
